items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: Three governors won on pausing data centers: TX, OH, GA = 40%+ of planned US capacity
items.idea: Democrats won governor races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia on promises to pause or slow data center construction; Evercore (via WSJ) says those states hold over 40% of planned US capacity, Axios says over half. 56% of voters called data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote (SSRS). One investor estimates 25-35% of next year's US build is at risk, and OpenAI leaders discussed resetting 2027 capacity.
items.angle: Capacity at risk is a number you can size against capex guidance. Compare to what hyperscalers have guided.
items.tweetA: Data centers were a top-tier ballot issue for 56% of voters. When did capex last poll like a school levy? The buildout now needs a permission slip, not just a power purchase agreement. $VRT $ETN $CEG
items.tweetB: 25-35% of next year's US data center build at risk, from three states that hold 40%+ of planned capacity. Your 2027 GPU shipment model probably assumes zero of that. $NVDA $AVGO

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: Thursday's rout: NDX -6.4%, SOX -12.3%, $2.5T gone, 3x chip fund -39% in a day
items.idea: Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% (worst since March 2020), chip index -12.3%, Nasdaq Composite lost ~$2.5T (about $1T from the Mag 7). Picks and shovels hit hardest: AMD -17%, Dell and Ciena -15%, Vertiv -14%, Coherent -13%, Quanta -12%, Comfort Systems almost -12%. Retail posted its biggest net-sell day since the pandemic and a triple-leveraged chip fund fell 39%. Yet S&P is only 6% off the high and +7% YTD.
items.angle: The damage was concentrated in the physical-buildout layer, not the hyperscalers. That dispersion is the trade.
items.tweetA: Comfort Systems, an HVAC contractor, fell 12% in a day on a ballot result. That's how crowded the physical AI layer got. The S&P is still only 6% off its high.
items.tweetB: A 3x leveraged chip fund lost 39% in one session while the S&P is -6% from the high. The index is fine. The plumbing underneath it is where the leverage lived. $SOXL $SMH

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: $300B of AI equity issued this year, $100B more queued. All 2025 US IPOs and follow-ons: $194B
items.idea: Tech giants, chip companies and AI clouds have sold or priced over $300B of new stock and mandatory converts YTD, with ~$100B more on tap, including a proposed $60B Meta ATM that could launch early 2027. All US IPOs and follow-ons across every sector in 2025 totalled $194B. Anthropic starts formal IPO marketing this week and lists the week of Nov 16; smaller cloud Iren already delayed upgrades on tight funding.
items.angle: Supply of AI paper is the variable nobody models. Anthropic's listing is the supply event to watch.
items.tweetA: AI issuers have sold 1.5x the equity that the entire US market raised in 2025, and it's November. Now add Anthropic and a $60B Meta ATM. The question isn't demand for AI. It's demand for the paper. $META $CRWV
items.tweetB: Iren pushing back chip purchases because funding is tight is the canary. Biggest AI listing ever lands the week of Nov 16, right into a market that just lost $2.5T in a day.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: Texas test case: Starbase annexed land before moratoria, SpaceX hedges with 6GW in Arizona
items.idea: Hinojosa takes office Jan 19 after campaigning to block new approvals; Abbott already paused grid connections and air permits through December audits. But Starbase controls its own zoning and annexed land before nearby towns passed moratoria, state environmental commissioners are Abbott appointees with years left, and SpaceX unveiled a proposed 6GW rural Arizona site the day after the election. Multi-GW Starbase plans include up to 1GW floating power at Brownsville and 700-800MW at Bastrop toward 10GW by 2027.
items.angle: Jurisdiction arbitrage is now part of the AI capex model. Behind-the-meter and annexation are the workarounds.
items.tweetA: Annex the land before the town can pass the moratorium. That's the new data center playbook, and it's genuinely clever. Regulatory arbitrage is now a line item in the capex plan.
items.tweetB: SpaceX announced 6GW in Arizona the day after Texas voted. Nobody is cancelling a buildout. They're moving it, and the winner is whichever state sells power fastest. $XEL $PNW

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: Anthropic ~$900B compute commitments on an $81B run rate; OpenAI banks $11B at $1.25T
items.idea: Parekh's demand argument: Anthropic alone is lining up close to $900B of compute commitments with a run rate around $81B and growing; OpenAI just raised $11B at a $1.25T valuation. AI investment is about 1.9% of GDP this year per Goldman, the biggest share of growth for a new industry since railroads.
items.angle: Commitments are 11x run-rate revenue. That ratio is what the IPO has to justify.
items.tweetA: $900B of compute commitments against an $81B run rate. That's 11x revenue locked in as fixed cost before the IPO prices. Bull or bear, that's the number the book-building is about.
items.tweetB: 1.9% of GDP is AI investment. Railroads peaked near 6-9% in the 1850s. We're either early or the comparison is wrong. Which one the market decides this month matters for $MSFT $AMZN.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Building Value over Time
items.title: Underpriced upside of a blue Congress: high-skilled immigration for AI labs
items.idea: Parekh argues the market is ignoring that a Democratic Congress is likely to be more open on H-1B caps and green cards for graduates, and US tech/AI is 'immigration powered'. He notes this despite Stephen Miller becoming White House Chief of Staff.
items.angle: Talent as the third constraint beside power and chips. Policy watch.
items.tweetA: Everyone is pricing the blue wave as a power-and-permits story. If Congress loosens H-1B caps, the scarcest input in AI, people, gets cheaper. Miller as chief of staff is the counterweight.
items.tweetB: Chips, memory, power, now voters. The fifth input nobody puts in the model is visas. A split government might fix the one constraint the executive branch made worse.

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: 41 local data center ballot initiatives. Voters rejected all but one.
items.idea: Authers quotes George Noble: 'That one number tells you more about the next two years than anything else.' Opposition looks organic. Gavekal's Louis-Vincent Gave: hyper-growth phase is over, first financially, more importantly politically; power drained from Trump, so 'building stuff' is no longer the priority. Counter: Larry McDonald thinks Hinojosa moves to the center because hyperscalers threaten to leave for Arizona or Mexico, setting up a semi relief rally.
items.angle: Two credible camps with opposite trades. Local vs state is the line to watch.
items.tweetA: 41 local data center votes, 40 'no'. When it goes to a ballot, AI loses almost every time. The industry bet on federal support, but the vetoes are local.
items.tweetB: Gave says hyper-growth is over for political reasons. McDonald says Texas folds because jobs leave for Arizona. Both can be right: slower in Texas, same total, different map. Trade the map. $CEG $VST

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: Vance posts the poll: voters want the Iran war ended. Oil -15% in a week to $98.30
items.idea: Republican defectors' top four reasons: end the war, cost of living, America First, change relationship with Israel. Robin Brooks: 'The war is now de facto over.' Oil fell 15% last week to $98.30 on peace hopes, with huge selloffs Monday and Wednesday. Contrarian risk: Miller's appointment suggests Trump may double down and a lame duck is dangerous. Futures a year out still above $80.
items.angle: Oil is trading a political signal, not a supply fix. Any collapse of talks reprices fast.
items.tweetA: Oil -15% in one week on a Vance tweet and a poll. The curve still has $80 a year out, so the market is pricing 'peace' and 'supply is back' as the same thing. They aren't. $XLE $USO
items.tweetB: The midterm result is arguably the most bearish catalyst for oil this year: it removes the escalation premium without adding a barrel. If talks fail the unwind is violent. $CVX $OXY

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: Third Trump 2.0 correction: NDX 13.5% below September peak; multiple lowest since Covid
items.idea: Authers: three corrections in two years (Liberation Day, Iran war, now the blue wave), all driven by presidential mistakes. Only two of 11 S&P sectors, tech and energy, suffered severe losses; five gained. The Nasdaq 100 trades at a blended 12-month forward multiple not seen since Covid's worst days. He calls it a potential buying opportunity unless political risks are profound.
items.angle: Both AI and oil, the two inflation drivers, deflated together. That's a macro regime tell.
items.tweetA: The two things pushing inflation and yields up, AI capex and oil, both just got politically capped in the same week. Good for the 10-year. Terrible for the two most crowded long trades.
items.tweetB: Three Trump corrections, three different causes, same pattern: the index falls, 5 of 11 sectors hold. If dispersion is the story, equal-weight vs cap-weight is the trade, not direction. $RSP $QQQ

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: SaaSpocalypse hasn't arrived: ServiceNow op margin 32.5%, +150bp vs guide. But $200B debt due in 2 years.
items.idea: Gap between Nasdaq 100 and S&P 1500 software 12-month performance has narrowed to almost nothing. ServiceNow's CFO says AI deployment drove >$1B annualized value and lifted operating margin 150bp above guidance; IBM and Adobe say similar. AI mentions on earnings calls have plateaued. Software forward EPS rises steadily. But ~$200B of software debt matures within two years, much raised near zero rates, with refinancing costs doubling.
items.angle: Software is using AI to cut costs, not to grow. Margin story with a refinancing overhang.
items.tweetA: ServiceNow beat its margin guide by 150bp using AI. Software isn't being eaten by AI, it's eating the headcount line. The $200B refi wall at double the coupon is the actual risk. $NOW $ADBE
items.tweetB: Software sold off with AI last week, as Authers notes. If AI sentiment turns negative and software margin benefit is what's real, the stocks don't need AI hype. Some of the oldest longs are cleaner than semis.

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: Prime-age unemployment at boom levels; Sahm Rule false alarm; Fed funds pricing 4.75% to 4.25%
items.idea: October unemployment unexpectedly fell (payrolls +165k, above all forecasts). Prime-age unemployment is at levels usually seen in booms. The Sahm Rule tripped in Aug 2024 and was a false alarm. At end-September investors priced fed funds above 4.75% next year; last week's selloff pulled that to about 4.25%. CPI due tomorrow.
items.angle: The Fed hike path is being priced off the equity tape. Stock weakness is doing the Fed's work.
items.tweetA: The Sahm Rule fired in 2024 and recession never came. A model that gave one false positive in 60 years just gave another, and rates traders are still pricing cuts in places. $TLT
items.tweetB: Funds rate priced 4.75% to 4.25% in five weeks, mostly because Nasdaq fell. Equity is the Fed's reaction function again. A strong CPI plus a bounce brings the hike pricing back. $SPY $ZT

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Morgan Stanley: record momentum drawdown, hedge fund exposure collapse, Wilson sees final innings
items.idea: Nick Savone's Global Reflections after the Nasdaq's worst day since the pandemic describes a record drawdown in tech momentum and an extraordinary reduction in hedge-fund exposure. Positioning is at levels historically tied to strong forward returns, earnings are resilient, and Mike Wilson thinks the correction may be near its final innings. Innes flags that the AI financing cycle, the Fed and the marginal buyer complicate it. Only teaser visible; rest paywalled.
items.angle: Clean-slate positioning plus hawkish Fed. The question is who the marginal buyer is.
items.tweetA: Positioning is at levels associated with strong forward returns, per Morgan Stanley, and the Fed is hiking in December. Both are true. The market has to decide which one drives the next 10% move. $QQQ
items.tweetB: Momentum didn't just fall, it posted a record drawdown. Funds that sold momentum because it hurt are the same ones who'll need to chase it back. That's the squeeze setup, if there's a catalyst.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Nvidia board investigates whether Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence honey trap
items.idea: Huang admitted an extramarital affair; the board launched an independent investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation involving a woman reportedly suspected by US authorities of Chinese intelligence links, a former exec at Singapore's Megaspeed International (scrutinized over chips reaching Chinese customers). No evidence of compromise so far, but congressional committees want answers, outside counsel is engaged, and there is no public succession plan. Nasdaq futures slipped as much as 1%.
items.angle: Key-person and export-control risk on the stock that carries the index. Headline-driven.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's board hired outside counsel to find out whether its CEO was targeted by Chinese intelligence. The company carrying the index has no public succession plan. That's a governance discount that isn't in 11x earnings. $NVDA
items.tweetB: The honey-trap angle is a distraction. The real exposure is Megaspeed, chips leaking to China through Singapore. A congressional committee investigating CEO judgment is the same committee writing export rules. $NVDA $AMD

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Microsoft reportedly declined to renew rented Oracle compute because older Nvidia hardware no longer met needs
items.idea: Innes cites Microsoft's decision not to renew rented computing capacity from Oracle, reportedly because the older Nvidia hardware was inadequate. Hyperscalers are getting selective about external cloud partners. He floats that Big Tech may be rewarded for spending less: lower capex improves free cash flow while suppliers suffer slower orders.
items.angle: Depreciation lives on GPUs get tested in the rental market first. Watch ORCL's remaining performance obligations.
items.tweetA: Microsoft let an Oracle GPU lease lapse because the Nvidia chips were too old. Hardware obsolescence is the one accounting assumption you can't hand-wave. Who holds the six-year depreciation? $ORCL $MSFT
items.tweetB: Capex down is bad for $NVDA and good for $MSFT free cash flow. The first CEO who says they're cutting wins the stock. The market is already trading that: hyperscalers fell less than suppliers.

items.title: Asia Monday: Nikkei +1.9% on SOX +4.2% bounce; Brent $98; BTC toward $75k; Dec hike ~80% priced
items.idea: MSCI Asia Pacific +0.7%, Nikkei up nearly 1.9% following Friday's 4.2% US semiconductor rebound. Brent trades around $98 on Iran diplomacy; dollar softer; Bitcoin recovering toward $75,000. Markets still assign nearly 80% probability to a December Fed hike after Friday's jobs, with CPI Tuesday as the test.
items.angle: Cross-asset snapshot ahead of CPI. 80% hike odds vs. Authers' 4.25% funds path is a gap to watch.
items.tweetA: BTC near $75k, Brent $98, Nikkei +1.9%, and 80% odds of a December hike. A hot CPI is the only print that matters this week and everything else is positioned around it. $BTC $SPY
items.tweetB: Fed hike odds near 80% while Nasdaq was just down 13.5% from peak. The hike path is the bigger risk to semis than any election. A soft CPI and the dip gets bought. A hot one and Thursday's low gets retested.

items.source: MacroEdge Research
items.title: MacroEdge: Dec hike 'priced in', hot CPI sends odds above 95%, 10Y up, France hit hardest
items.idea: Weekly note: December hike is now priced in, a hot CPI Tuesday would push odds above 95%, and the 10Y is setting up for another leg higher that probably hits the EU, particularly France, hardest. Argues bond vigilantes used the 'growth scare' to recharge and there are no sound solutions to Western fiscal positions. Also: PPI Friday Nov 13; Cisco and Applied Materials report this week.
items.angle: Contrast with Innes (80%) and Authers (4.25% path). Three sources, three hike odds.
items.tweetA: If the 10Y breaks higher on hot CPI, the French OAT-Bund spread is the pressure valve. Sovereign fiscal issues don't care about the AI correction. $FXE
items.tweetB: Innes says 80% priced. MacroEdge says 'priced in', 95% on hot CPI. Authers has funds rate at 4.25%. Same market, three numbers. Whoever is wrong on hike odds is wrong on duration. $TLT

items.source: MacroEdge Research
items.title: 'The race to call the bottom' - rage on X at cycle highs, nobody properly hedged
items.idea: MacroEdge expects one more leg lower to find the local low, then 2-3 months of calm. The race to call the bottom is at levels never seen in this 2023-present cycle, with an unusual level of anger on X this weekend as a sentiment barometer, and he thinks nobody actually has proper hedging. NVDA is flagged as precarious for the whole cycle even if a reflex rally comes; Wednesday evening 'buttered up' tech egos before Thursday's spike.
items.angle: Sentiment contrarian indicator. Hedging gap is the claim; verify with options skew.
items.tweetA: Everyone is calling the bottom the same weekend. When the crowd fights over who called it first, I've learned to wait. Check skew before you buy. $VIX
items.tweetB: Spike in vol arrived Thursday as MacroEdge predicted. The thing to watch: if hedges weren't on, there's no put demand to unwind into a rally. That makes bounces violent in both directions. $VIX $UVXY

items.source: MacroEdge Research
items.title: Claim: US 'on the verge of losing' status as global naval superpower
items.idea: In the intro the author references his Oil and Gas Research note from last week saying the US is on the verge of losing its status as a global naval superpower, calling it a genuinely concerning development. No detail in the preview; the supporting analysis sits in the paid report.
items.angle: Shipbuilding/naval capacity thesis is a defense-supply-chain angle. Needs the underlying note.
items.tweetA: One line in a macro note: the US is near losing naval superpower status. If true, shipbuilding capacity is a bigger constraint than munitions. Who's actually building hulls? $HII $GD
items.tweetB: The Iran war is a naval and logistics test as much as an air one. If the market is pricing peace but carrier and shipbuilding capacity are the real constraint, defense spending isn't a trade, it's a decade.

items.source: BowTiedBull
items.title: Bids filled on weekend selloff; first opening in a year to build a position
items.idea: BowTiedBull says the AI slowdown has been called since late June, expects extremely volatile Anthropic IPO if it lists this year, and notes some limit bids hit in the weekend selloff. He argues there is finally an opening to build a position for the first time in over a year, given tech-cycle history; specific levels are behind the paywall.
items.angle: Contrarian-bull on a self-described bear-aligned call. Details paywalled.
items.tweetA: The people who called the slowdown in June are now building positions. That's the signal I'd watch: bears turning into scale-in buyers at lower prices.
items.tweetB: Anthropic IPO into a market that just lost $2.5T in a day. Either it prices the bottom, or it's the supply that makes it. I want to see the order book before the narrative. $NVDA

items.source: Ben Pouladian / BEP Research
items.title: NVDA at $179: 11.3x FY28, 8.4x FY29 earnings. The Apple 2007-2012 analogue
items.idea: With NVDA ~$179 overnight, consensus puts it at roughly 11.3x FY2028 and 8.4x FY2029 earnings. Apple's net income went from $3.5B (FY07) to $41.7B (FY12) while its forward multiple fell from ~29x to ~10x; NVDA's went $4.4B (FY23) to $120.1B (FY26) while its multiple declined. Buybacks: NVDA $40.1B in FY26 vs. Apple's $78-95B a year; NVDA added a $150B authorization. Author plans to add Monday morning. Subscriber chat note; analyst charts referenced.
items.angle: Valuation case. Must be paired with the governance headline. Author is long.
items.tweetA: Apple 2012: earnings up 12x, multiple down from 29x to 10x, stock still did fine for a while, then didn't. NVDA is on the same path. The multiple compressing is the trade only if earnings arrive. $NVDA $AAPL
items.tweetB: A $150B buyback authorization is permission, not cash spent. NVDA bought $40B last year. If it wants to defend the stock during a board review, it has to spend in a window when insiders are restricted. Watch the 10b5-1.

items.source: Trading Mindset & Data (TMAD)
items.title: Liquidity index turned negative after September FOMC while retail bought dips
items.idea: TMAD argues thin liquidity amplified the selloff and downside may remain. Its liquidity index trended down and turned negative shortly after the September FOMC while the market kept rising and retail kept buying dips. New options heatmaps show open interest and GEX by strike/expiry; example: DRAM memory ETF saw a massive OI change in Nov 20 $40 calls. Indicator paywalled; author is cautious on a sharp bounce alone.
items.angle: Liquidity as a leading indicator. The DRAM ETF call OI is a specific memory positioning signal.
items.tweetA: The liquidity index went negative in September, six weeks before the crash. Price kept going up. Liquidity doesn't tell you when, only that the floor is thin. $SPY
items.tweetB: Massive new open interest in Nov 20 $40 calls on the DRAM memory ETF. Someone is paying for upside in memory right after it fell hardest. Either a hedge on short memory or a very early bottom call. $DRAM $MU
